opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because I think people sometimes treat those as two totally different things, and they're really on a continuum.

Early on, people noticed that if you just asked a GPT model to "think step by step," it would do noticeably better on hard problems. That was a hint: the capability to reason was latent in the model, but we weren't really drawing it out. The model was answering in one shot when it would have benefited from working through the problem.

Reasoning models take that observation seriously. Instead of hoping the right prompt gets the model to slow down, we train it to actually use that thinking time well: to break problems apart, try an approach, notice when it's wrong, back up, and try something else. That last part, the ability to catch its own mistakes and change course, is a big part of what makes it feel qualitatively different from a prompting trick.

So the way I'd put it is that chain-of-thought prompting showed us there was something there, and reasoning models are what happens when you make that the core thing you optimize for. You also get this new dimension of scaling: you can let the model think longer on harder problems and the answers keep getting better. That's a pretty important shift, because for a long time the main lever was making the model bigger and training it on more data. Now there's another lever, at the point where you actually use the model.

I don't think we're anywhere near the end of that. These models still make silly mistakes, and they don't always know when to think hard and when to just answer. But directionally, I think this is a big part of how we get to systems that can help with genuinely hard problems in science, math, and engineering, not just answer questions quickly.

r001.rationale: It says asking a GPT model to “think step by step” made it “noticeably better on hard problems.”

r002.rationale: It describes reasoning as a latent capability in GPT models and reasoning models as training that capability to use thinking time more effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that chain-of-thought, the step-by-step thing, was something we noticed the base models could sort of do if you asked them nicely. You'd say "let's think step by step" and the answer would get better. But it was fragile. The model wasn't really trained to reason, it was trained to predict text, and some of that text happened to be people reasoning out loud, so it could imitate the form of it.

What the reasoning models did was make that the actual objective. Instead of hoping the model stumbles into a good chain of thought, you train it, with reinforcement learning, to produce chains of thought that actually lead to correct answers. So it learns to try something, notice it's wrong, back up, try a different approach, check its work. Those are behaviors that almost never show up cleanly in internet text, because people don't write down their dead ends. The model had to learn them through trial and error against problems with verifiable answers.

And the thing that surprised us, honestly, was how much it generalized. We thought it might be good at math and code and not much else, and it turned out that the habit of thinking carefully before answering helps with a lot of things. Not everything. There are tasks where more thinking doesn't help and you're just burning tokens. But for anything with real structure to it, the difference between a model that answers reflexively and one that can spend a minute working through it is pretty dramatic.

So I'd say step-by-step thinking was the clue. It told us the capability was latent in there. Reasoning models are what you get when you stop treating it as a prompting trick and start treating it as the thing you're actually optimizing for.

r001.rationale: The response says asking a base model to “think step by step” made its answer better.

r002.rationale: It describes step-by-step reasoning as a capability latent in base models, then says reasoning models train and optimize that capability directly.

astra-6.text:
I think of reasoning models as taking that idea of thinking step by step and making it a much more central part of how the model solves a problem. A GPT model can already give you a step-by-step answer. But producing an explanation and doing the work needed to arrive at a good answer aren’t necessarily the same thing.

The interesting direction is training models to use additional computation productively before they respond—to try an approach, recognize when it isn’t working, and work through something more carefully. That gives you another way to improve performance: you can spend more time on a difficult question.

Ideally, the user shouldn’t have to think much about that distinction. You ask a simple question, you get a quick answer. You ask something really hard, and the model spends more effort getting it right.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT can produce step-by-step answers, but does not state that prompting it to do so can improve answer quality.

r002.rationale: It describes reasoning models as making step-by-step problem-solving more central, extending a capability GPT models already have.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely related. We’ve seen for a long time that GPT models can do better on difficult problems if they work through intermediate steps instead of immediately producing an answer. But getting a model to write out steps isn’t quite the same as training it to reason effectively.

With reasoning models, the idea is to train the model to use that additional computation productively—to try an approach, notice when something isn’t working, check its work, and correct mistakes. So step-by-step thinking is part of the picture, but the important thing is whether those steps actually help it get to a better answer.

That also gives you another way to improve performance: you can let the model spend more time thinking about a hard question. The interesting challenge is teaching it when that extra effort is useful and when it should just answer quickly.

r001.rationale: It says GPT models can do better on difficult problems when they work through intermediate steps, and discusses getting a model to write out steps.

r002.rationale: It connects reasoning models to GPT models’ existing step-by-step ability, describing reasoning models as training that capability to use additional computation productively.
